newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW says can't challenge Canadian vote.
newsitem.headline: CAW says can't challenge Canadian vote.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers union president Buzz Hargrove said on Thursday the union cannot challenge a Canadian government order that CAW members vote on a restructuring plan for ailing Canadian Airlines Corp.
"The one decision we have made after an agonizing night is that there is no way that we can challenge this legally," Hargrove told a news conference.

Hargrove said the union planned to continue negotiating with Canadian and the government for a better deal. The CAW is the only one of six unions at Canadian that has not accepted a restructuring plan the airline called critical to its survival.
The CAW represents 3,700 ticket agents at Canadian, Canada's second biggest airline.
Hargrove said the union had not yet decided whether it would recommend acceptance or rejection of the restructuring plan, which includes wage concessions.

"We are now agonizing over whether or not we recommend rejection (of the restructuring package) by our members," said Hargrove, who has argued against the need for more wage concessions by Canadian employees.
Hargrove said he expected most CAW members to back whatever the bargaining committee recommended.
"If that is to ratify, they'll ratify. If that is to reject it, they will reject," Hargrove said.
"I am not afraid to let the workers vote," he added. "We are absolutely confident that if we recommend rejection, our members will endorse that in large numbers."

He said he would use the rest of today to see if he could secure a better deal from Canadian and the goverment. The CAW wants the goverment to increase its aid package to Canadian and re-regulate Canada's airline industry.
The CAW represents 3,700 ticket agents at Canadian, Canada's second biggest airline. The carrier has about 16,400 employees.
Canadian Labor Minister Alfonso Gagliano, in an extraordinary move on Wednesday, invoked a little-known section of Canada's labor vote to force the CAW vote.
He said talks were at an impasse "and 16,000 jobs are at stake." The restructuring package for Canadian is contingent on support from all six of its unions.
